kp.k: Licensing framework specifies foundational legal knowledge and practical skills
kp.d: NCBE specifies examination content rather than making claims about AI or its effects on legal employment. The scope applies to July 2026 and February 2027. Its broader July 2026–February 2028 framework combines eight doctrinal fields with issue analysis, investigation, counseling, negotiation, client management, research, and writing. These are stated assessment requirements, not findings about workplace performance or technological change.
qs: The content scope outlined here applies to the July 2026 and February 2027 administrations of the NextGen Uniform Bar Examination (NextGen UBE).

Foundational Skills: issue spotting and analysis, investigation and evaluation, client counseling         and advising, negotiation and dispute resolution, client relationship and management, legal         research, legal writing and drafting

Foundational Concepts and Principles: business associations and relationships, civil         procedure, constitutional law, contracts, criminal law and constitutional protections of accused         persons, evidence, real property, torts

kp.k: Doctrinal recall and resource application remain distinct assessment requirements
kp.d: The outlines distinguish starred topics, assessed without legal resources, from unstarred topics, which may be assessed with or without resources. Without resources, unstarred topics require recalled understanding sufficient to recognize the issue. Supplied resources require efficient analysis and application. The supplied text does not reliably display topic-level stars, so particular topics cannot be assigned to those categories here.
qs: Topics followed by a star symbol require an examinee to rely solely on recalled knowledge and      understanding of the topic; they will be tested without provision of legal resources.
Topics without a star symbol may be tested with or without provision of legal resources.
When legal resources are provided within the test, the examinee will be expected to demonstrate their ability to efficiently analyze and apply the legal resources to answer the question or questions.

kp.k: Skills assessment extends beyond the core doctrinal knowledge base
kp.d: Other doctrinal fields can provide contexts for testing foundational skills without requiring examinees to develop prior substantive knowledge in them. Family law and trusts and estates will appear in this resource-supported form on every examination from July 2026 through February 2028. Separately, criminal offense and defense elements are tested using supplied statutes.
qs: Other areas of legal knowledge may be included to provide context for testing Foundational Skills, but examinees are not expected or required to develop a base of knowledge in those areas.
For these questions, relevant legal resources (e.g., statutes, regulations, and case law) will be provided.
Family law and trusts and estates will appear in this way—embedded within skills-focused questions—on every exam from July 2026 through February 2028.
Elements of crimes and defenses will be tested on the basis of provided statutes.

kp.k: Analysis includes factual investigation and assessment of competing positions
kp.d: Defined tasks require identifying outcome-relevant law and facts, applicable standards and burdens, strengths and weaknesses, missing information, and probable outcomes. The framework treats factual development and evaluation of both sides as examinable legal skills; it does not describe automated performance of these tasks.

kp.k: Client objectives constrain advice, negotiation, and legal strategy
kp.d: Client-facing assessment requires selecting lawyering strategies under relevant rules while accounting for the client's objectives, interests, and constraints. Tasks include identifying negotiation terms, evaluating benefits or drawbacks of dispute resolution, explaining whether objectives are attainable, and determining strategies to identify client needs and achieve stated goals.

kp.k: Research competence includes authority, updating, relevance, and sufficiency
kp.d: Research tasks encompass defining research questions, recognizing ambiguity, choosing efficient methods and search terms, distinguishing authoritative weight, comparing material facts across opinions, updating sources, and deciding whether available sources suffice to complete an assignment. These are legal research assessment requirements, not AI benchmarking or verification requirements.

kp.k: Writing competence encompasses drafting, revision, and original legal analysis
kp.d: The writing tasks cover client correspondence, pleadings, affidavits, contract provisions, memoranda, persuasive documents, and discovery documents. Examinees may need to identify defective language, explain needed changes, suggest revisions, select supporting affidavit language, and formulate original legal analysis consistent with facts, rules, and client objectives.

kp.k: Selected professional rules are assessed through client-facing integrated questions
kp.d: Specified ABA Model Rules may be assessed within Group B integrated question sets, not standalone multiple-choice sections, and require recalled knowledge without supplied resources. Coverage includes terminology, competence, specified representation and confidentiality provisions, diligence, communication, current-client conflicts, meritorious claims, specified candor provisions, truthfulness, and dealings with represented and unrepresented persons. Comments and cross-referenced provisions not separately enumerated are excluded. This is an examination scope, not a change to professional regulation or an express AI-competence mandate.

kp.k: Digital evidence and electronic transactions fall within doctrinal scope
kp.d: Civil procedure expressly includes e-discovery, metadata, and large volumes of electronically stored material. Contracts includes the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act and effectiveness of electronic signatures and records. These establish technology-related examination coverage but do not assert AI adoption, productivity gains, or job displacement.
